units.translation: But upon those who have been orphaned, fasting hunger presses.
ἀπόσκημμα [prop, support]: ἀπέρεισμα [support]. Aeschylus in Argeioi (fr. 16).
to drag away, tear away, lead away
to drag away, tear away, lead away
It seems I will drag you away, having torn you by the hair.
And from my eyes drips a mournful shame of tears.
Standing near and standing apart at a distance.
But ruin stands apart from friends.
Alone of the gods, Persuasion stands apart.
The god does not stand apart from just deceit.
The tower keeps off the crowd of enemies.
As the sun departs into night.
But I hate the opposite word to these.
But an unexpected, sudden death deprived him of life.
Do not hold out gain to me and then deprive me.
May lord Zeus deprive me of a marriage that is ill for a husband.
(Thus Porson for πήματος τρέψαι νόσον [to turn away the disease of suffering].)
We shall try to turn away the suffering of the disease.
to turn away the disease of suffering
Is there no escape for him from this fortune?
to strip and take away, snatch away
to strip and take away, snatch away
By whom he is stripped of scepter and honors.
And fear was upon all the barbarians, who had wandered from their judgment.
Other copies have ἀπέταμες [you cut off]. See Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 1731.
But now if he pays for the blood of those before.
He paid for this fully, having sacrificed upon fresh offerings.
May great Nile turn away your insolent outrage, making it unseen.
I fear and turn away from the terror of the citizens.
If you saw anything bad, take for yourself an averting of these things.
Wishing to sacrifice a cake to the averting gods.
Such a graceless grace, an averter of evils.
An averting pollution, to be prayed away.
You spoke reasonably in my absence.
In the absence of the noble lion.
It has been decided to bring forth a hateful Muse.
First we were bringing forth a renowned army (Wellauer: renowned armies).
Having destroyed these chicks of the father.
Having destroyed the offspring of the eagle.
In time, fear perishes for mortals.
And by a woman he perished in life.
And by the destruction of seed.

The true spelling of the word is confirmed by Pollux 3, 56, who interprets ἀποφύλιον [tribeless] as τὸν φυλὴν μὴ ἔχοντα [the one having no tribe]. In Suidas two similar words are confused, ἀποφύλιοι [tribeless], which means ξένοι [strangers], and the Homeric ἀποφώλιοι [vain, useless], which he explains by ἀπαίδευτοι [uneducated]: on this see Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 1780.
